stories.title: Japan launches its MMX mission to bring back the first sample from Mars' moon Phobos
paragraphs: Japan's Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission launched today, Oct. 19, on an H3 rocket from Pad-2 at Tanegashima Space Center's Yoshinobu Launch Complex at 3:41 p.m. EDT, which is 12:41 p.m. PT and 4:41 a.m. on Oct. 20 in Japan, Space.com reports. Space.com says it was the 10th flight of the H3, developed by JAXA and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, and that the rocket flew a nominal trajectory over the Pacific, dropping its four solid boosters just before the two-minute mark and its payload fairing about 80 seconds later. According to Space.com, the plan called for the upper stage to fire a second time for a trans-Mars injection burn about one hour and four minutes after liftoff, with MMX released about a minute after that burn ended, roughly 368 miles (592 kilometers) above central Africa. ESA says the mission is led by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) together with NASA, the French space agency CNES, the German Aerospace Center DLR and ESA, and it will be the first mission to collect a sample from Phobos and bring it back to Earth.

ESA says MMX will take around a year to reach Mars, entering orbit around the planet in August 2027 and orbiting Phobos from September 2027. After studying Phobos and Deimos from a distance, it is to release the 25-kilogram Idefix rover in early 2029; ESA notes Phobos' gravity is so low that Idefix will weigh the equivalent of 15 grams there. ESA says the main spacecraft will land on Phobos in 2030, and a return module will deliver at least ten grams of Phobos material in a capsule that lands in Australia in 2031. The mission carries 11 science instruments, seven on the main spacecraft and four on the rover, according to ESA. Space.com adds that MMX will spend about three years in the Martian system, making two separate touchdowns on the 14-mile-wide (22 km) Phobos to collect samples and later flying past the smaller moon Deimos several times before leaving for Earth in November 2030.

ESA says the moons may be asteroids captured into Mars orbit or the remnants of debris thrown into orbit by a giant collision on Mars, and that samples are needed to find out. Space.com quotes NASA MMX program executive and program scientist Tom Statler, from an Oct. 15 statement: "Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds." Space.com also reports that MMX was originally supposed to launch in 2024, but problems with the H3 rocket kept it grounded until the next Earth-Mars launch window, which comes once every 26 months.

Science News reports that if MMX succeeds it will be the first mission to reach Phobos, after three earlier Russian spacecraft failed, and that the returned rocks may even contain stray grains blasted off Mars itself. The magazine notes that NASA's plan to fetch the Perseverance rover's samples is in limbo after the U.S. Congress cut funding for that follow-on mission, which has made scientists keen on even an indirect look at Martian material. NASA Johnson Space Center planetary scientist Michael Zolensky told Science News that 15 percent of the sample will eventually go to Johnson, adding, "A few grams of sample are going to be a real bonanza for scientists." Space.com reports that NASA's contributions include the MEGANE gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, a pneumatic sampler built by Honeybee Robotics and Deep Space Network support, about $87 million in total through the end of the mission.

stories.title: OpenAI says its newest models are far better at COBOL, Fortran and other low-resource programming languages
paragraphs: OpenAI said on Oct. 19 that its latest model advances bring stronger capabilities for building and migrating software in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran and Visual Basic. In its announcement, the company explains that these languages have less code and documentation for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure. OpenAI cites figures that COBOL supports more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions and 95% of ATM transactions, and that Fortran is used in weather forecasting and nuclear reactor safety analysis. The company says the work is guided by feedback from developers and enterprise customers who told it that coding models often struggle with these languages.

To measure progress, OpenAI says it built two evaluations. MultiLangBench asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch in each of 20 programming languages, checking the results against the reference SQLite implementation with tests adapted from SQLite's own test suite. According to OpenAI, GPT-6 Astra reached an average test pass rate of 87.4% across the 20 languages at maximum reasoning effort, up from 26.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol, with gains in every language tested. OpenAI reports COBOL rising from 10.9% to 72.1%, Fortran from 21.4% to 83.5% and Visual Basic from 27.5% to 89.4%, with COBOL remaining the hardest. It says the lower-cost GPT-6 Luna reached 40.3% at an estimated average API cost of $0.77 per sample, compared with $3.48 for GPT-5.6 Sol, about 78% lower.

The second evaluation asks models to migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python or Rust, and counts a migration as successful only if hidden tests requiring byte-for-byte matching outputs all pass. OpenAI gives the example that COBOL's fixed-point arithmetic discards extra decimal digits unless rounding is requested, so a rewrite that rounds instead can run without errors while producing different financial results. On this test, OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol scored 86.6% at low reasoning effort, compared with 5.4% for GPT-5.6 Sol at the same setting, and reached 97.9% at higher reasoning effort, which the company says brings the evaluation close to saturation.

OpenAI says it is releasing the MultiLangBench setup and test suite on GitHub, along with results for each language. The company adds that applying these capabilities to production software still requires expert review and testing against a system's business rules and dependencies. These benchmark results are OpenAI's own reported figures.

stories.title: Mathematicians say an OpenAI proof of the 'quasi-Riemann hypothesis' looks correct, calling its implications 'staggering'
paragraphs: Number theorists who have spent the past two weeks studying an AI-generated proof released by OpenAI on Oct. 6 largely agree that it is correct, Quanta Magazine reported on Oct. 19. The proof claims to settle the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a weaker version of the Riemann hypothesis, which has been open for more than 160 years and concerns how prime numbers are distributed. Jared Duker Lichtman of Stanford University called it "the most significant AI-for-math achievement so far, by quite a margin," and Maksym Radziwiłł of New York University told Quanta the implications are "staggering," adding that "the vast majority of consequences of RH already follow from quasi-RH."

Quanta explains that the Riemann hypothesis says all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function have a real part of 1/2, while the quasi version only asks for proof that they lie in a vertical strip narrower than the known one between 0 and 1. According to Quanta, OpenAI announced two versions: one dated Sept. 30, 199 pages long and formally verified in the Lean programming language, placing the zeros between 1/8 and 7/8, and a 49-page version completed almost a week later, not yet formally verified, placing them between 1/12 and 11/12. Mathematicians have focused on the shorter paper, which Quanta says is the only one of OpenAI's Oct. 6 papers to have been edited by a person; OpenAI told the magazine, "The paper is the result of work from everyone at OpenAI."

Radziwiłł told Quanta that both papers are "horribly written," falling well short of the field's standards of clarity, but that he can now sketch the argument in half a page. Experts quoted by the magazine say the proof introduces no new concepts and instead combines long-known ideas, including obscure objects called metaplectic forms and a formula that Radziwiłł and Alexander Dunn of the Georgia Institute of Technology proved in 2021. Quanta reports that Princeton's Peter Sarnak has repurposed a course he is teaching this semester to study the proof, and that he said he won't be satisfied it is "a Theorem" until humans check and understand all the details.

According to Quanta, mathematicians expect the result to establish many other results in number theory, geometry and theoretical computer science, but they are skeptical that the same techniques can reach the full Riemann hypothesis. "It seems most likely to me that once mathematicians have fully internalized the new methods and worked through their implications, we will still feel as far off from the full Riemann hypothesis as we were before," Will Sawin of Princeton told the magazine, adding, "But I am not certain of this."

stories.title: Anthropic commits 5% of its shares to a new Public Benefit Fund that can grow as the company's value rises
paragraphs: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, announced on Oct. 18 that it is committing a portion of its shares to a new entity called the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. According to the company, 5% of Anthropic's shares will be committed now, subject to stockholder approval, and the board may add another 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline.

Anthropic says that as a public benefit corporation, most of its mission work happens inside the company, including AI safety and interpretability research, applied biomedical research, and discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. The company says the new fund will have more flexibility and scale, and gives examples such as large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations. It names the labor-market impact of AI as one area, noting it has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing that issue.

The fund is being set up as a wholly owned LLC rather than a 501(c)(3), which Anthropic says allows it to adjust between different forms of giving. The company states that none of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad. Anthropic contrasts the structure with the common tech-industry practice of escalating executive compensation awards, saying it is directing that equity to the public benefit instead.

Anthropic says the move builds on earlier pledges: its co-founders pledged at founding to donate 80% of their equity, and about half of its employees take part in an equity donation match program. Combined with the new fund, the company says roughly 20% of its shares will be dedicated to the public good, and it plans to share more about the fund's structure, governance and valuation milestones in the coming months.

stories.title: Four Google DeepMind Gemini 4 Argon agents beat Minecraft on their own, defeating the Ender Dragon in about 27 hours
paragraphs: A team of four AI agents running on Google's Gemini 4 Argon model has beaten Minecraft without human help, according to a Google DeepMind paper posted on arXiv on Oct. 15. The paper says the agents were placed in a sandboxed survival world with a single goal, defeating the Ender Dragon, and did it in 27 hours and 14 minutes.

According to the paper, each agent controlled a player through Mineflayer, an open-source library, and coordinated with its teammates through in-game chat and a shared memory. The authors say no one assigned roles or wrote game logic: the agents planned, wrote and debugged every program themselves. The game was Minecraft Java Edition 1.20.4 in survival mode on Easy difficulty, in a randomly generated world with cheat commands disabled and no human input during the run. Researchers could watch on a live dashboard and pause or stop the run, but the paper says they had no cause to intervene.

The paper reports that the team wrote 2,783 programs, exchanged 229 messages and died 605 times along the way. According to the authors, the agents divided the work among themselves, posted coordinates and warnings to teammates in shared memory, and recovered each other's items after deaths. The paper estimates the whole session cost about $810 at Gemini 4 Argon's introductory list price, or $1,620 at the standard price.

The authors call it, to their knowledge, the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents using only the standard Mineflayer library, without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans. For comparison, the paper notes that HowLongToBeat's median for Minecraft's main story is 45 hours for human players and the random-seed speedrun record is under seven minutes, and that the agents played as a team of four on Easy difficulty, through programs rather than a screen and keyboard. The paper also includes a section on the limits of the result.

stories.title: Physicists report evidence of 'pair density waves' in uranium ditelluride that persist even above its superconducting temperature
paragraphs: A team led by researchers at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign reports compelling evidence of pair density waves on the surface of the metal uranium ditelluride, according to a ScienceAlert article published Oct. 18 at 7 p.m. PT (Oct. 19 UTC). The results appear in the journal PNAS. ScienceAlert explains that in a superconductor, electrons pair up into so-called Cooper pairs that move with zero resistance, and that pair density waves, predicted in 2007, are an exotic state in which those pairs form repeating patterns as they move.

ScienceAlert reports that the patterns were found to persist outside the standard superconducting state, something it says has never been seen before. Uranium ditelluride becomes a superconductor below about 2.1 kelvin and is thought to be a rare spin-triplet superconductor. "Pair density waves are the Cheshire Cat's grin of superconductivity," physicist Eduardo Fradkin of the University of Illinois told the outlet. "They are the vestige that remains once the phase itself has disappeared."

According to the article, the team used a custom-made, high-quality sample and a vector magnetic field scanning tunneling microscope, which can apply magnetic fields in multiple directions. Physicist Zhen Zhu said varying the field's strength and direction along with temperature let the team build confidence that the behavior was intrinsic, and physicist Vidya Madhavan said the modes persisting above the superconducting temperature is a prediction that had not been convincingly observed before.

ScienceAlert notes that the finding does not mean bulk superconductivity is happening in the material at higher temperatures, but says it helps physicists understand how Cooper pairs can exist outside the conventional superconducting state and could help research toward higher-temperature superconductors. Physicist Julian May-Mann of Stanford told the outlet that confirming a pair density wave requires both high-quality experimental data and careful theoretical analysis.
